title: Matched fsx acceptance on a real mounted cowfs against a native control
note: This is the wave g4 gate (fsx). It is not docs/v1-benchmarks.md's g4, which is the tree-walk gate.

tool.name: fsx
compile_notes: -D_GNU_SOURCE, -D_FILE_OFFSET_BITS=64, -std=gnu11, -funsigned-char, -fno-strict-aliasing and -Wall are the flags xfstests' own include/builddefs.in puts on every C file.
-include getopt.h and -include linux/kernel.h are needed because ltp/fsx.c calls getopt_long and roundup without including their headers. The source stays unmodified.
-DXFS is deliberately not defined: without xfsprogs headers it turns the -x preallocation block into a compile error. It gates only that block, and this gate never passes -x.
tool.why_this_source: fsx/ was removed from xfstests before the oldest tag this gate could pin; ltp/fsx.c is the surviving upstream file, unchanged since the xfstests 4.x era.
declared_not_covered: AIO (-A): libaio is not linked, so the binary's usage text omits the flag
io_uring (-U): liburing is not linked, so the binary's usage text omits the flag
copy_file_range (-E): HAVE_COPY_FILE_RANGE is undefined in fsx-config-linux.h
xattrs, xfsprealloc, atomic writes, dontcache io: the corresponding macros and flags are compiled out

manifest.note: Approved before execution. run-fsx-gate.py refuses a binary whose digest is not this one, and records the check in the meta row. The three source digests are what build-fsx.sh verifies before it compiles.
manifest.rebuild_note: A rebuild on another host produces a build-specific digest. The pin is against this binary, not a promise of reproducibility across toolchains.

caps.comment: fsx's own defaults are a 256 KiB file and a 64 KiB operation; the op cap is lowered to 16 KiB so a seed stays modest. Byte caps are enforced by the runner, which refuses a data file over max_file_bytes and reports the total written per arm.
caps.caps_note: max_file_bytes and max_op_bytes reach fsx as -l and -o and the runner refuses a data file larger than max_file_bytes. max_bytes_written_per_arm is the whole-run budget per arm: the declared batch is 15 seed pairs, so 15 x 2 x max_file_bytes, and a run that exceeds it is reported FAIL after the fact rather than refused mid-run, because the per-file cap is the one fsx enforces and the total is this gate's own budget. recorded_op_window is fsx's own LOGSIZE, the ring buffer it keeps the recorded operations in. A mode whose difference has to be located runs within it; a mode compared by digest does not need to.

matched_flags_note: -f flushes and invalidates the cache after every I/O, so the arms read through the filesystem rather than through the page cache. -F -H -z -Y -C -I -u disable fsx's fallocate-based operations: allocate, punch hole, zero range, write zeroes, collapse range, insert range and unshare range. They are disabled on BOTH arms so the operation mix stays matched, and they are disabled because the cowfs FUSE mount answers ENOTSUP to every fallocate mode, measured by bench/fsx-gate/fallocate-matrix.py. Disabling them on both arms keeps the arms comparable; disabling them on the cowfs arm alone would make the result look worse than it is.

modes.name: smoke
modes.why: The first real run: one fixed seed, small op count, one operation mix on both arms, before any batch.

modes.name: matched
modes.why: The declared batch: ten seeds, one operation mix on both arms, so the two files must end byte-identical. The fallocate family is disabled on BOTH arms, which is what makes the two operation streams identical; that is a declared subset of fsx's capability set, not a weakened acceptance. At 20000 operations the recorded stream is a tail, so this mode relies on the digest comparison, which covers the whole run, and not on locating the first divergence.

modes.name: sync
modes.why: One seed with -y so every change is synchronized.

modes.name: full
modes.why: fsx's own default mix with every capability it finds, which is how the hole coverage of this mount is measured rather than assumed. This mode cannot PASS: the mount has no fallocate, so fsx records a different operation stream on each arm and the two files are not comparable. It runs at 10000 operations rather than 20000 because fsx keeps only the last 10000 operations it records, and locating where the two arms part company needs the whole stream, not a tail. fsx's exit status is recorded; execution equivalence is UNMEASURABLE and stays that way until the mount implements fallocate. Issue 103.

required_op_types_note: fsync is not listed anywhere: fsx selects op = rv % OP_MAX_FULL and OP_FSYNC == OP_MAX_FULL, so no random run can ever record an fsync operation. The gate found that out by failing on it, and the coverage moved to the sync mode's -y flag and to the fsync_readback probe.

probe.why: fsx probes fallocate modes itself and prints one line per mode it disables. The runner probes the same operations directly as well, so an unsupported hole operation carries its own errno evidence instead of only fsx's stderr.

accept.why: g4 is 'mounted fsx no worse than native'. Native is the control, so the bar is that the cowfs mount produces exactly what native produces for the same declared inputs, and that fsx itself finds nothing wrong on the mount.
rules: the two arms are on different filesystems, verified by st_dev, so the cowfs arm really is the mount
executed operations equal the declared op count on both arms
in a mode with one operation mix, the recorded stream (.fsxops) is byte-identical across arms
in a mode with one operation mix, the data file is byte-identical across arms (size and sha256)
in a mode that lets fsx use every capability, every stream difference traces to a capability the mount is recorded as lacking
a fresh process that opens the file after fsx exits reads the same sha256
after the daemon restarts on the same store, every cowfs data file still hashes the same
no mode was skipped, truncated or reduced without an explicit unsupported reason recorded
an empty or missing result never passes
